description: Fog, smoke, sun, wind, fire, fireflies, lightning, crystal and moon are the forms that come first in yoga, bringing about the manifestation of brahman.
When the fivefold quality of yoga (earth, water, fire, wind, space) arises, there is no sickness, old age or death for one who has gained a body made of the fire of yoga.
Lightness, health, freedom from craving, clearness of complexion, pleasantness of voice, a pleasant odour and little urine and excrement — the first results of yoga.
As a mirror stained with dust shines when cleaned, the embodied one seeing the reality of the self becomes one, fulfilled and free of sorrow; by the self as by a lamp he sees brahman.
The light beyond heaven, the same as the light within the person, is perceived as warmth in the body when touched and heard, with the ears closed, as a roaring, like the crackling of a blazing fire.
The digestive fire within is heard as a sound when the ears are covered; when one is about to depart one no longer hears it (a sign of approaching death).

Closing the ears with the thumbs, practitioners hear the sound of the space within the heart, likened in seven ways — rivers, a small bell, a bronze vessel, a wheel, croaking frogs, rain, a voice in a sheltered place — and pass beyond it into the soundless brahman.
Piercing the darkness with Om as arrow, one sees brahman flashing like a whirling firebrand, sun-coloured, powerful, beyond darkness.
When through the dissolution of the mind one sees by the self the self, subtler than the subtle, shining, one becomes selfless (nirātman) — called the mark of liberation.
The teaching about brahman with respect to the gods: that which flashed in the lightning — 'ah!' — and made one blink — 'ah!'.
When the five senses of knowledge stand still together with the mind and the intellect does not stir — this is called the highest state.
In dream the person is his own light; there are no chariots, roads or joys there but he creates them; others see his playground, no one sees him.

Like a tired falcon returning to its nest, the person reaches the state without desire or dream; embraced by the intelligent self like a man by a beloved woman he knows nothing within or without; father is no father, Vedas no Vedas; he has crossed all sorrows.
He becomes the ocean, the one seer without duality — the world of brahman, the highest bliss on a fraction of which beings live.
When one is fully asleep, serene, seeing no dream, one has entered the channels and no evil touches one, for one is filled with light.
In dream the mind experiences its greatness, seeing again the seen and unseen, heard and unheard; overcome by light (tejas) it sees no dreams, and happiness arises in the body.
The fourth: neither inward- nor outward-knowing, not a mass of cognition, unseen, ungraspable, the stilling of the world, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual.

At death the self gathers the particles of energy into the heart; the person in the eye turns away; 'he is becoming one', they say; the tip of the heart lights up and by that light the self departs through the eye, the head or another part of the body.

The appearance of the person is like a saffron-dyed cloth, white wool, an indragopa beetle, a flame, a white lotus, a sudden flash of lightning; to one who knows this, glory comes like a flash of lightning.
When the seer sees the golden-coloured maker, the Lord, the person, the source of brahman, he shakes off merit and evil and attains supreme equality.
Rising from the body, the serene one reaches the highest light and appears in his own form; he moves about laughing and playing, not remembering the body.
For one who knows the honey-doctrine the sun neither rises nor sets; for him it is always day.
The one who sees (thus) does not see death, nor sickness, nor sorrow; he sees all and obtains all.
The knower, moving through the worlds, eating what he wishes and taking what form he wishes, sings 'hā u! I am food, I am the eater of food ... I have overcome the whole world'.
Vāmadeva, lying in the womb, knew all the births of the gods and, breaking out 'as a falcon', became immortal.
Triśaṅku's declaration: 'I am the mover of the tree ... I am shining wealth, wise, immortal, imperishable' (words partly obscure).
